audience_name: A blogger with an existing site and an RSS feed, finally switching their email send-out off Mailchimp after putting it off for a while

dossier.audience_name: A blogger with an existing site and an RSS feed, finally switching their email send-out off Mailchimp after putting it off for a while
dossier.orientation: Buttondown is browser-based software this blogger can use to automatically turn their existing RSS feed into scheduled or per-post emails, instead of relying on Mailchimp for that same job.

setup_conditions: Choose an RSS-to-email cadence in the dashboard: per new item, weekly, or monthly (R2, R3).
For a weekly or monthly digest, build the email template using a loop over the feed's items (R4).
A digest-style template cannot be paired with the per-new-item cadence; doing so results in the email not sending (R5).
unverified_requirements: Whether the resulting RSS-to-email setup excludes bundled CRM-style list-management features this audience wants to avoid is not established by the selected evidence.
Whether the tracking-pixel opt-out (E3) applies to opens on automated RSS-to-email sends specifically, as opposed to manually composed emails, is not established by the selected evidence.
decision_gaps: Which Buttondown plan tier includes RSS-to-email automation, and at what price — the ledger names 'free' and 'Basic' offers but not which unlocks this feature or its cost, which is central to a cost-driven switcher's decision.
Does disabling tracking pixels (E3) also suppress tracking on emails generated by the automated RSS-to-email pipeline, or only on manually sent emails?
Can the RSS-to-email cadence and digest template be configured via the API or CLI (E24) rather than only through the dashboard?
defining_need_fit.caveat: The audience's core defining action — replacing Mailchimp's RSS-to-email send-out with an equivalent — is covered by Buttondown's automatic feed-pull-and-send mechanism and its documented cadence/template mechanics, but digest and per-item cadence are mutually exclusive, and absence of CRM bloat and scope of the tracking opt-out for automated sends are not confirmed.
defining_need_fit.why: E5 establishes the core mechanism (pull an RSS feed, send it automatically); R2–R5 establish the cadence and template options and their one documented mutual-exclusion exception, together covering the blogger's stated migration task.

ranked_relevance.why: A customer's firsthand account of switching an RSS-to-email setup from Mailchimp to Buttondown mirrors this exact audience's situation and reports it as cheaper, more flexible, and less cluttered.
States the core mechanism this audience needs: automatically pulling an RSS feed and sending it to subscribers, replacing the function they currently get from Mailchimp.
Directly answers the researched complaint that a Mailchimp-based RSS digest kept tracking subscribers despite opting out, via an option to turn tracking pixels off.
A customer's timed comparison of setting up RSS-to-email in Buttondown versus Mailchimp supports the ease of the same kind of migration this audience is making.
Documents the per-new-item cadence option, one of the two cadence mechanisms underlying the RSS-to-email capability this audience needs.
Documents the weekly cadence option, matching the weekly-digest cadence one source in this audience explicitly relied on Mailchimp for.
Documents how a digest-style RSS email template is built, the mechanism needed if this audience wants a multi-post weekly send rather than one email per post.
Documents the necessary exception that a digest template cannot be combined with the per-new-item cadence, a condition on the digest mechanism above.

problem_fits.caveat: Buttondown's RSS-to-email automation (E5) with configurable per-item or weekly/monthly cadence (R2, R3) and a tracking-pixel opt-out (E3) covers the audience's narrow stated need, but a digest template cannot be paired with the per-new-item cadence (R5), and the selected evidence does not confirm Buttondown excludes other CRM-style features the audience wants to avoid.
problem_fits.why: Matches the audience's explicitly stated requirement for an automatic RSS-to-email feature and its complaint that a Mailchimp-based digest kept tracking subscribers after opt-out.

problem_fits.caveat: One customer who made the same RSS-to-email migration calls Buttondown cheaper (E9), and Buttondown's commercial terms (newsletters billed only by subscriber count, no surcharge on paid subscribers or sponsorships, a free tier described as generous) support lower overhead, but no evidence in the ledger states a specific price or confirms savings against the $326/month this audience cites.
problem_fits.why: Addresses the cost-driven motivation to leave Mailchimp, though the magnitude of savings is not established by the selected evidence.

segment_objections.objection: Will Buttondown still track my subscribers even after I ask it not to, the way Mailchimp did with my RSS digest?
segment_objections.answer: Buttondown lets users turn tracking pixels off, and is described as GDPR-compliant with no data collection about owners or subscribers by default.

segment_objections.objection: Will Buttondown actually be cheaper than Mailchimp for someone running more than one blog, given no specific prices are shown here?
segment_objections.answer: A customer who made this exact RSS-to-email migration calls Buttondown cheaper, and Buttondown lets you run unlimited distinct newsletters while charging only for total subscribers.

evidence.claim: Buttondown lets users turn tracking pixels off so subscribers are not tracked.
evidence.verbatim: I LOVE being able to turn tracking pixels off. I didn't even realize this was an option when I signed up and am SO HAPPY to not track people.

evidence.claim: Buttondown's RSS-to-Email feature took about 30 minutes to set up for one customer, versus the time it took to figure out the equivalent feature in Mailchimp.
evidence.verbatim: I just tested the RSS to Email feature for one of my blogs and it was incredibly easy to set up. It took me about 30 mins to figure out the same feature in Mailchimp.

context.subject: Buttondown RSS to Email feature compared with Mailchimp
context.conditions: one customer's personal setup-time test of both tools
context.limitations: single user's timed impression, not a controlled benchmark

evidence.claim: Buttondown can take an RSS feed, automatically pull in its content, and send it to subscribers.
evidence.verbatim: The killer feature for me: Buttondown will take an RSS feed then automatically slurp up the content (in their words) and then send it to our subscribers.

evidence.claim: Buttondown has a free version of its product that one customer described as generous.
evidence.verbatim: Hands down the easiest way to run a newsletter - and the free version is generous!

context.subject: Buttondown free plan
context.limitations: no specific free-tier limits, credits or figures stated

evidence.claim: A customer who switched their RSS-to-email provider from Mailchimp to Buttondown found Buttondown cheaper, more flexible, and less cluttered.
evidence.verbatim: This long weekend I fulfilled a long-standing promise to myself to switch my RSS-to-email provider from Mailchimp to Buttondown, and it's been such a great experience. It's cheaper, more flexible, less cluttered, and it's run by Justin Duke who is just delightful and answered a bunch of my questions over the weekend (even though I asked him to please not!).

context.subject: Buttondown versus Mailchimp for RSS-to-email
context.conditions: one customer's personal migration experience, Rian van der Merwe, Director of Product at PagerDuty
context.limitations: subjective comparison with no specific prices or figures cited

evidence.claim: Buttondown does not charge newsletter owners extra for paid subscribers, so they keep all of the revenue they make.
evidence.verbatim: The best part? We won't charge you extra for paid subscribers, so you'll keep all of the revenue that you make.

evidence.claim: Buttondown is GDPR-compliant and does not collect any data about newsletter owners or their subscribers by default.
evidence.verbatim: Buttondown is GDPR-compliant and then some. We don't collect any data about you or your subscribers by default.

context.subject: Buttondown data collection and GDPR compliance

evidence.claim: Buttondown takes no cut of newsletter sponsorships; creators keep 100% of every sponsorship, minus Stripe's processing fee.
evidence.verbatim: Buttondown doesn't take a cut: you keep 100% of every sponsorship (minus Stripe's processing fee).

evidence.claim: Buttondown lets users create as many distinct newsletters as they'd like, charging only based on total subscriber count.
evidence.verbatim: Create as many distinct newsletters as you'd like – you're only charged for your total subscribers.

context.subject: Buttondown unlimited newsletters pricing
context.conditions: charged by total subscriber count, not number of newsletters

evidence.claim: Buttondown's RSS-to-email automation can be configured to trigger per new post as it is published.
evidence.verbatim: You can have trigger a new email every time a new item is published in your RSS feed.

context.subject: Buttondown RSS-to-email cadence option
context.claim_scope: one of three selectable cadence options for RSS automation
context.conditions: Buttondown checks the RSS feed every thirty minutes, so triggering is not instantaneous
context.limitations: This cadence cannot be combined with a digest-style template (see separate restriction)

evidence.claim: Buttondown's RSS-to-email automation can instead be configured to trigger weekly on a chosen day and time, matching a weekly-digest pull preference.
evidence.verbatim: You can trigger a new email every week, on a day and time of your choosing.

context.subject: Buttondown RSS-to-email cadence option
context.claim_scope: one of three selectable cadence options for RSS automation
context.conditions: For weekly cadence, the automation only triggers if there is a new item in the RSS feed since the last check

evidence.claim: Buttondown's RSS-to-email templates can be built as a digest that loops over multiple feed items collected during the chosen cadence.
evidence.verbatim: If you want to send a digest of multiple blog posts, you'd start by iterating over the list of items in the feed.

context.subject: Buttondown RSS-to-email digest template
context.claim_scope: template-building behavior for digest-style RSS emails
context.conditions: Requires a weekly or monthly cadence setting; relies on a {% for item in items %} loop structure

evidence.claim: A digest email cannot be used with the per-post ('every new item') cadence, confirming that the digest format only works with the weekly/monthly cadence options.
evidence.verbatim: You cannot create a digest email when the schedule is set to "every time a new item appears". This would result in the email not being sent.

context.subject: Buttondown RSS-to-email digest/cadence compatibility restriction
context.claim_scope: configuration restriction tying digest templates to non-per-item cadences
context.conditions: Applies when the RSS automation's schedule is set to trigger on every new item
context.limitations: Documentation does not state what error or notification the user sees beyond the email not being sent
